# What effect does statistics anxiety have on attainment?
## Effect Size Summary

d = `r grades_d`, 95% CI [`r grades_cor_result$conf.int`], based on N = `r N`.


## Summary of Analysis Approach (max 100 words)





## Details of the Analysis
The data is from an International Multi-Centre Study of Statistics and Mathematics Anxieties and Related Variables in University Students (the SMARVUS Dataset) @SMARVUS_paper. This dataset contains survey responses from N = 12,570 students from 100 universities in 35 countries, collected in 21 languages. They attempted to measure anxieties (statistics, mathematics, test, trait, social interaction, performance, creativity, intolerance of uncertainty, and fear of negative evaluation), self-efficacy, persistence, and the cognitive reflection test, and collected demographics, previous mathematics grades, self-reported and official statistics grades, and statistics module details.

We chose to only include UK universities in our analysis because it is the country with the most observations, at 2962, making up around 24% of the data. Additionally, this ensures that our results aren't affected by any other cultural differences between subjects that could affect grades or maths anxiety.
 
Six "attention checks" were built in to the survey, which we used to filter out any participant that weren't paying attention to the questions, as this would invalidate their other responses (10.36%). Additionally, we filtered out students who responded "No" to the question "Please indicate whether you feel you have answered the previous questions carefully and truthfully" (1.01%), as well as students that responded "Yes" to the question "You have just answered three reasoning problems. Did you look any of the answers up online?" (1.93%). 

Additionally, we filtered our data to only include Psychology undergraduate students, as they made up the majority of degree majors at the UK universities surveyed (93.0%), and this would also improve the strength of our comparisons between students, as different course demands and difficulty levels would also affect anxiety levels.

We also noticed that the amount of missingness varied largely across degree years, with the majority of observations being in first and second year and over half the grades for these observations being missing. The grade data from the few observations in 3rd and 4th year were almost completely missing.

``` {r na_grades_by_degree}
grade_na_bydegree
```

We can also examine the distribution of the grades to see that the majority lie around 65%. 
``` {r grades_histogram}
grades_hist
```
### Statistics Anxiety
To measure statistics anxiety, the STARS (Statistics Anxiety Rating Scale) tool was used. This typically contains 51 items, though here only the 3 anxiety subscales of the STARS were used, giving 23 items. Each is to be rated on a 5-point scale, with a 1 indicating "no anxiety" related to the stated item, and a 5 indicating "a great deal of anxiety". We calculated a total STARS score for each participant by summing their responses for the 23 items (excluding the attention check question at the end of the section). The possible range for total STARS score is 23-115,with a higher score indicating greater statistics anxiety.

The distribution of STARS scores is shown below. The mean STARS score was calculated as 71.26, and the median was 71, with a standard deviation of 17.77. Observed scores ranged from 28 to 115. A check was carried out to ensure that part answers to the STARS section (i.e. anyone who had answered some of the STARS questions but not all) were not included so as not to skew the sum, but no partial answers were found, so all responses were included.

```{r} 
STARS_hist
```
### Relationship Between Statistics Anxiety and Attainment
To investigate the relationship between statistics anxiety and attainment, we looked at the association between participants' total STARS score and their grades in their statistics modules (in percentage).

Below is a scatter plot of total STARS score against statistics module grades. We can see the fitted regression line and 95% confidence interval showing the estimated statistics module grade at each STARS score. 
```{r}
STARS_attainment
```
This plot suggests there is a weakly negative relationship between statistics anxiety and statistics module grades. The predicted grade at a STARS score of 28 is around 70%, while for a STARS score of 115 it is around 62%. Using Pearson's correlation coefficient to measure the strength of the relationship, we found that the correlation was -0.14, with a p-value below 0.05 (p=0.00007), and a 95% confidence interval of [-0.21, -0.07]. Taken together, these results indicate a weak but statistically significant negative relationship between statistics anxiety and attainment. 
However, due to the nature of the study, we cannot conclude whether this relationship is causal or whether other factors contributed to or explain the observed relationship.
We additionally converted the correlation coefficient into our Cohen's d effect size value, and found an effect size of `r grades_d`. We converted from correlation as our variables are continuous and not naturally split into two groups, therefore directly calculating cohen's d using group means was not appropriate. We considered splitting our data manually into two groups ("high" and "low" anxiety) but decided against it as the splitting would be arbitrary, and we were concerned about loss of information.
